subject: Economics
description: Revenue/capital receipts, fiscal/revenue/primary deficit, FRBM, public debt, transfers

questions.stem: The FISCAL DEFICIT is best defined as:

options.option_text: The difference between revenue receipts and capital receipts
Total expenditure minus total non-borrowed receipts
Revenue expenditure minus tax-only revenue receipts
The gap between corporate tax and direct tax collection

questions.explanation: Fiscal deficit = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts (excluding borrowing). It measures the total borrowing requirement of the government. Important for macro-stability — funded by market loans (G-Sec auctions), small savings, external loans. India's FY24 fiscal deficit ≈ 5.6% of GDP (target was 5.9%); FY26 budget targets 4.4%. Distractor 1 = a balance-sheet split, not deficit. Distractor 3 ≈ revenue deficit but excludes non-tax revenue. Distractor 4 = arbitrary, not a defined deficit.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: REVENUE DEFICIT differs from fiscal deficit in that it covers only:

options.option_text: All borrowings minus repayments to the central bank
Revenue expenditure exceeding revenue receipts
Capital expenditure minus capital receipts only
Foreign loans subtracted from external grants

questions.explanation: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts. Indicates that the government is borrowing for current consumption (not asset creation) — generally considered fiscally unhealthy. The FRBM Act, 2003 originally targeted ZERO revenue deficit but has been repeatedly missed. Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD) — excludes grants for capital-asset creation given to states. Distractor 1 = not a defined deficit. Distractor 3 ≈ capital deficit (rare term). Distractor 4 = arbitrary.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Fiscal deficit plus interest payments due in the year
Fiscal deficit minus interest payments due in the year
Revenue deficit minus capital expenditure on infrastructure
Total tax revenue minus combined direct + indirect tax

questions.explanation: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments. Strips out the legacy of past borrowings (interest on old debt) to show whether CURRENT government operations are themselves in deficit. A primary surplus means new borrowing is being used only to service old debt; revenue + spending are matched. India's primary deficit has historically been positive; budget targets aim to bring it to ~0%. Distractor 1 reverses sign. Distractors 3 and 4 are unrelated formulas.

questions.stem: The FRBM Act, 2003 was enacted to:

options.option_text: Regulate foreign exchange transactions across the border
Set fiscal targets and ensure inter-generational equity in public finances
Bring all public sector banks under single government ownership
Authorise direct cash transfers to below-poverty-line households

questions.explanation: FRBM (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management) Act, 2003 — sets quantitative fiscal targets (originally fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP, zero revenue deficit). Aimed at fiscal discipline + inter-generational equity (today's borrowing must not unfairly burden future taxpayers). Has 'escape clause' for unusual periods (war, natural calamity, structural reform); was triggered during COVID. N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP target instead of just fiscal-deficit target — debt anchor of 60% (Centre + States combined). Distractor 1 = FEMA, 1999. Distractor 3 = bank nationalisation (1969, 1980).

questions.stem: Direct taxes (income tax, corporate tax) are NOT shareable with states under the divisible pool because:

options.option_text: They are collected by the states themselves and not the Centre
They actually ARE part of the divisible pool (this premise is false)
States already get a 100% share of all direct taxes by law
Direct taxes are constitutionally exempt from any inter-state sharing

questions.explanation: Direct taxes (income tax + corporate tax) are CENTRAL taxes BUT they ARE part of the divisible pool. The 15th Finance Commission (2021-26) recommended states receive 41% of the divisible pool. So the question's premise is FALSE — and option B correctly flags this. Note — surcharge and cess collected by Centre are NOT shared (this is a long-standing state grievance, since the share of cess + surcharge has risen sharply). Other central taxes in pool: GST (CGST), customs duty.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: PUBLIC DEBT of the Government of India has two components — INTERNAL debt (borrowings within India) and EXTERNAL debt. The bulk of India's public debt is:

options.option_text: External, borrowed mostly from the IMF and World Bank
Internal, borrowed largely through dated G-Sec auctions
Equally split, roughly half internal and half external
External, borrowed mostly from sovereign-wealth investors

questions.explanation: India's public debt is OVERWHELMINGLY internal (~95% in rupees, ~5% external in dollars/yen). Most internal debt is via dated government securities (G-Sec) auctioned by RBI to banks, insurance companies, mutual funds. External debt — small share, mostly from World Bank, ADB, JICA (Japan), bilateral. Low external-debt share insulates India from currency depreciation risk on debt servicing — a key strength compared to many EMs (Argentina, Turkey, Sri Lanka). Distractor 1 — opposite of true. Distractor 3 — far from 50-50.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The ratio of CESS + SURCHARGE in the Centre's gross tax revenue has RISEN sharply in recent years because:

options.option_text: Cesses are recurring annual taxes formally part of the divisible pool
Cesses and surcharges are not shared with states under Article 270
States voluntarily contribute additional cess for development
The constitution requires that 50% of cess always flows to states

questions.explanation: Article 270 — central taxes are shareable with states; HOWEVER, surcharges (Article 271) and cesses (Article 270 proviso) are EXCLUDED from the divisible pool. Centre keeps 100% of cess + surcharge → strong fiscal incentive to RAISE THESE rather than core taxes. Examples: Health & Education Cess (4% on income tax), GST Compensation Cess, Road & Infrastructure Cess on petrol/diesel, Krishi Kalyan Cess (now subsumed). State governments and Finance Commissions repeatedly call for cess + surcharge to be brought back into the divisible pool. Distractor 1 — opposite of true. Distractor 4 — invented.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: All tax revenues, loan repayments received by the Centre, and most non-tax receipts flow into a single fund established by the Constitution. Under which Article is this fund created?

options.option_text: Article 265 — prohibiting taxation without legislative authority
Article 266 — establishing the Consolidated Fund and Public Account
Article 267 — creating the Contingency Fund of India for emergencies
Article 268 — providing for duties levied by Union but collected by States

questions.explanation: Article 266 of the Constitution establishes both the Consolidated Fund of India and the Public Account of India. Article 265 (no taxation without law) is a common distractor but concerns the authority to levy taxes, not the fund itself. Article 267 creates the Contingency Fund, and Article 268 covers Union duties collected by states — altogether different provisions.

questions.stem: A government budget classifies receipts as either revenue or capital. Which of the following CORRECTLY falls under CAPITAL RECEIPTS in the Union Budget?

options.option_text: Recovery of loans previously advanced to state governments
Corporation tax collected from domestic companies during the year
Dividends received from public sector enterprises and banks
Non-tax revenue earned from Union government services and fees

questions.explanation: Capital receipts either create a liability (borrowings) or reduce a financial asset (loan recoveries). Recovery of loans reduces the government's outstanding financial assets, qualifying it as a capital receipt. Corporation tax, PSU dividends, and non-tax fees are revenue receipts — they recur periodically and do not alter the government's asset or liability position.

questions.stem: The Union Budget 2011–12 introduced a new deficit indicator called Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD). ERD is derived from the Revenue Deficit by deducting which item?

options.option_text: Interest payments made on internal and external public debt
Grants transferred to states and UTs for creation of capital assets
Capital expenditure incurred directly by the Central Government
Revenue expenditure on centrally sponsored schemes and subsidies

questions.explanation: ERD = Revenue Deficit minus grants given to states/UTs earmarked for capital asset creation (e.g., roads under PMGSY). Although such grants appear as revenue expenditure in the Centre's accounts, they produce capital assets at the sub-national level. Subtracting them reveals the truly consumptive portion of the revenue deficit. Interest payments and subsidies remain inside the revenue deficit and are not excluded in computing ERD.

questions.stem: The Constitution distinguishes between 'Charged' and 'Voted' expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India. Charged items may be DISCUSSED in Parliament but cannot be voted down. Which of the following is a CHARGED expenditure?

options.option_text: Grants-in-aid to state governments under Article 275 of the Constitution
Expenditure on MGNREGS wages and materials under Demand for Grants
Salaries and allowances of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
Central allocation for construction of national highway infrastructure

questions.explanation: The Constitution (Article 148) places the salary of the CAG beyond the annual vote of Parliament to protect the independence of the audit function. Other charged items include the President's emoluments, SC judges' salaries, and debt servicing charges. Grants under Article 275, MGNREGS allocations, and highway construction are submitted as Demands for Grants and are subject to Parliament's vote — a frequent source of confusion in exams.

questions.stem: Performance budgeting and Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB) represent two distinct approaches to public expenditure management. Under ZBB, the mandatory starting point for each annual budget cycle is:

options.option_text: The previous year's sanctioned outlay adjusted for inflation and growth
Fifty percent of the previous year's actual expenditure as a floor limit
The amount recommended by the Finance Commission for the plan period
Zero — every expenditure must be freshly justified without reference to past allocations

questions.explanation: ZBB mandates that every programme or activity be justified from scratch each year as if it did not exist previously — the base is zero, not last year's budget. Option A describes conventional incremental budgeting, which ZBB was designed to replace. India experimented with ZBB in the 1980s. Options B and C are not standard descriptions of any recognised budgeting methodology, making them effective distractors for candidates who conflate ZBB with other deficit-control measures.

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of India extends Ways and Means Advances (WMA) to the Central Government under Section 17(5) of the RBI Act, 1934. Which statement MOST accurately describes WMA?

options.option_text: Long-term concessional credit lines drawn under multilateral aid agreements
Grants released by RBI from the Currency and Finance Reserve for deficit financing
Temporary overdraft bridging short-term cash-flow mismatches, repayable within 90 days
Market-stabilisation bonds issued jointly by RBI and government to manage liquidity

questions.explanation: WMA are short-term advances (not bonds, not grants) given by RBI to tide over temporary timing mismatches between Central Government receipts and payments within a fiscal year. They carry interest at the repo rate and must be repaid within 90 days; if the limit is breached, the government must issue treasury bills to the RBI. Option A confuses WMA with multilateral loans (World Bank/IMF). Option B mixes it with the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), and Option D correctly names MSS but wrongly labels it as WMA — a classic paper-setter trap.

questions.stem: Article 292 of the Indian Constitution governs the borrowing powers of the Union Government. What condition does Article 292 impose on Union borrowings?

options.option_text: Such limits as Parliament may fix by law, borrowing only on security of the CFI
Prior approval of the National Development Council and the Planning Commission
Ceiling prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee
Ratification by at least half the state legislatures within sixty days of sanction

questions.explanation: Article 292 authorises the Union to borrow money upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of India, within limits Parliament may by law fix — operationalised today by the FRBM Act, 2003 and its fiscal deficit targets. Option C is wrong because the RBI's MPC is a monetary policy body with no authority over public borrowing ceilings. Option B references the now-defunct Planning Commission. Option D applies the Article 368 constitutional amendment procedure to borrowing, which is constitutionally incorrect.
